Twenty-six comments

This is a common session tune most often played in G, but it was apparently originally written in F, which is my preferred key (I cheat and capo my zouk at the 3rd!)

This was composed by Larry Redican, who I think was born in Dublin, and brought up in Boyle (Co. Roscommon) before he left for New York. The Culfadda gets spelt a lot of different ways (e.g. Culfodda, Kilfadda, Kilfodda) but Culfadda is the correct spelling. There is a place called Kilfadda, but this is a red herring. The tune was named after Culfadda in Co. Sligo where Larry’s mother came from.

Another name for this tune is “The Cruel Father”. I’m guessing that when Larry went to New York he played his tune and when asked the name of it they couldn’t understand his accent. Only a guess :-)

↳ Posted by Dr. Dow on March 16th, 2003.

Redican’s source.

The 1883 tune book “Ryan’s Mammoth Collection” (aka Cole’s “1000 Fiddle Tunes”) includes a reel called “Hit or Miss,” the turn of which is nearly identical to that of Redican’s “Culfadda” (though in C rather than F). Cape Breton fiddler Winston Fitzgerald played “Hit or Miss,” as can be heard on a cassette of 78s and private recordings produced by Paul Cranford some years ago. The first parts of the two tunes are not at all similar.

“Cruel Father,” by the way, was the title that appeared on Four Men and a Dog’s debut recording “Barking Mad.”

Re: The Culfadda

Cúl Ḟada refers to long hair going down the back, possibly in a braid. I believe the Cúl Ḟionn, also a beautiful air, refers to blond locks. Carolan describes Suave Mabel Kelly’s coolin in his Planxty to her. The coolin and coolfada are Irish hairstyles, that may have looked something like these: https://www.google.ie/search?q=irish+hair+braid&dcr=0&source=lnms&tbm=isch&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjC_sKzq9jYAhWrK8AKHft1AgwQ_AUICigB&biw=970&bih=1185#imgrc=Uja4gcDgQDtrbM:

The Culfadda, X:10

This is my preferred setting of the tune which I first learned from hearing it on the radio and called “Larry Redican’s”. I believe it was recorded from Larry Himself when Ciarán Mac Mathúna visited the US for his Job of Journeywork programme on Radio Éireann in the 1960s. I and my friends always played it in the key of G major, but it may well have been originally set in F.

The Culfadda, X:11

hi everyone,

Here is a transcription of the version that Kevin Burke plays with Ged Foley on the 2006 album “In Tandem,” which I’m partial to. They spell it “The Culfodda,” and it’s preceded by “Never Was Piping So Gay” and followed by “The Graf Spee.” It seemed distinct from the other F major versions posted here so far with the daring high A it ascends to in the second repeat of the B section, which I like. He repeats the A section with a very slight variation, which I went ahead and transcribed, but it’s basically the same both times through; the B section, though, has a quite distinct variation that makes it stand out.

I’ve been in love with this tune ever since hearing Maurice Lennon play it in Galway one night long ago. He called it “Larry Redican’s.” He recorded a lovely version on the compilation “Within a Mile of Kilty,” in which he plays it on a viola in the key of C a deep rich fourth below this version. I didn’t transcribe it cuz it was too low to play on a standard tune fiddle, but you should take a listen if you like the tune.

Re: The Culfadda

Location, location, location!
There’s only 20 km between Boyle, Co. Roscommon (of ‘The plains of the Boyle’ fame), a.k.a. Larry Redican’s birthplace, and Ballymote (of ‘The famous Ballymote’) fame.
Looking at the map of Sligo, the landscape is dotted with names we recognise readily from tunes: Killavil, Redhill, Kesh, etc. Fascinating stuff.
Culfadda, Co. Sligo lies just south of Ballymote.
According to brendankeane (and https://www.logainm.ie/en/s?txt=Culfadda&str=on) it means ‘The long wood’ (and not ‘the long ’‘bottom end’’ (as can be found in place names such as Cúltrá, Coolcullen, etc). Now I know.
